## Review

**7 out of 10, Effective.** Presentation quality, judged with the SlideDeck Co review heuristic (https://slidedeck.co/review-methodology/). The ask, the evidence and the merit of the idea are not rated.

The deck has a clear, consistent system: blue title bars that state the takeaway, a chart or image below, a source line, and a section divider every so often, so the 72 pages I saw are easy to navigate (slides 3, 12, 30). Most charts are readable and well matched to the claim, such as the stacked bars on slides 15 and 25 and the market cap tables on slide 7, and the then-and-now panels on slides 32 to 45 make the enterprise case at a glance. The weaknesses are real: many slides carry tiny footnotes and dense tables (slides 50, 51, 55), some chart labels are small (slide 69), several pages are plain italic text with an empty title bar (slides 20, 23, 27), and the slide 1 and 2 covers do not match the rest of the deck. As a long reading document it works well, but as a spoken presentation it asks a lot of the audience.

**Worth keeping:** Keep the takeaway-style title bars, the consistent source line, and the then-and-now panel layout with a one-line benefit caption (slide 32).

**Most useful repair:** Replace the empty blue bars on the statement slides with real headlines or remove them, and enlarge the small table text and footnotes on slides 50, 51 and 55.

**What would change the score:** I would cut or split the densest comparison tables and trim the long run of near-identical pages so the deck keeps momentum.

## Summary

The deck opens with a title slide, a conference-specific cover and an outline that lists eight sections: internet adoption, key internet trends, re-imagining enterprise and consumer behaviour, America's evolving work environment, big internet markets in China and India, public and private company data, one more thing, and an appendix. It starts with user growth from 1995 to 2014, tracing internet and mobile penetration with simple pie charts and then comparing company market capitalisations across two decades in a ranked table. The middle sections use a recurring structure of a headline-style title, a chart or table, and a short source line, and the enterprise section pairs a 'then' and 'now' panel for each software category. Later sections cover messaging platforms, user-generated content, drones, cyber security, labour market statistics and the growth of on-demand work. The deck is long, and most of its slides are dense data pages rather than visual statements. Slides worth studying include the outline, the market capitalisation comparison, and the then-and-now enterprise panels.

## Questions about this deck

**How many slides does the Mary Meeker, Kleiner Perkins Internet Trends 2015 deck have?**

The deck has 197 pages. The outline on slide 3 lists eight sections, from internet adoption through to the appendix.

**What does the Mary Meeker, Kleiner Perkins deck say about company market capitalizations?**

Slide 7 compares the top 15 public internet companies by market capitalization, stating 1995 @ $17 Billion and 2015 @ $2.4 Trillion. The totals on that slide are $16,752 MM for December 1995 and $2,415,867 MM for May 2015.

**How is the Mary Meeker, Kleiner Perkins deck structured?**

Slide 3 is the outline, listing eight sections: Internet, Key Internet Trends, Re-Imagining Continues, America's Evolving Work Environment, Big Internet Markets = China / India, Public / Private Company Data, One More Thing, and Ran Outta Time Thoughts with the Appendix. The middle sections repeat a headline-style title, a chart or table, and a short source line.

**What internet user figures does the Mary Meeker, Kleiner Perkins deck give for 1995 and 2014?**

Slide 5 states that internet users grew from 35MM+ in 1995, at 0.6% population penetration, to 2.8B in 2014, at 39% population penetration. Slide 11 adds that internet user growth was +8% in 2014 versus +10% in 2013.

**Layout**

Full-width blue title bar across the top (about 12.5% of slide height) with the title left-aligned at about 3.8% from the left edge, vertically centred in the bar. A centred bold subtitle sits below the bar, above a white framed panel holding the timeline chart that spans roughly 5.5% to 95.9% of slide width. The footer has the @KPCB logo at bottom left, a small source line beside it, and the page number at bottom right.

**Visuals**

One diagram: a horizontal timeline titled 'Evolution of Content Discovery, 1975 – 2015, per Nielsen' (the title is printed as the subtitle above the panel). Axis: a horizontal blue band carrying year labels 1965, 1970, 1975, 1980, 1985, 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015 at evenly spaced ticks, with no units. Two thin grey horizontal lines run across the chart, one above the band (about 58% of slide height) and one below (about 64.5%). Above the upper line, small open circles with light blue outlines mark events with vertical light-blue stems to labels: DVR (about 1998), HD DVD & Blu-Ray (about 1999), Satellite radio (about 2002), Time-shifted viewing (about 2003), Facebook (about 2004), 7th gen game console (about 2005), Twitter (about 2006), YouTube (about 2007), Netflix streaming (about 2008), Hulu+ (about 2009), Smart TV (about 2010), Tablet (about 2010), Instagram (about 2010), Streaming radio (about 2011), 8th gen game console (about 2012). Below the lower line, open circles with stems mark: VCR (about 1977), Cable (about 1979), AOL (about 1984), DBS Satellite (about 1992), Yahoo (about 1995), Google (about 1998), Broadband (about 1999), HDTV (about 2002), VOD (about 2006), Apple TV (about 2007), Smartphone (about 2007), Roku (about 2008), Amazon Prime Instant Video (about 2012), Chromecast (about 2013). Events are not connected by arrows. No legend and no highlighted points; all circles and labels are the same style, with no colour coding.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF slide background, with a blue #00689D title bar at the top. White slide with a #00689D (steel blue) title bar. Title in ArialMT regular, white #FFFFFF, about 4.4% of slide height (cap height about 3.1%). Subtitle in Arial bold, black #000000, about 3.3% of slide height, centred. Chart labels are Arial bold black #000000, about 1.8% of slide height. Year labels are white bold on a bright blue band #0099D8. Timeline lines are mid grey #6D6E71, about 0.3% of slide height thick. Event circles are white fills with light blue #2AA6DE outlines and stems in the same blue. The chart panel is white with a soft grey drop shadow. Page number is grey #353B37 and the source line is black. Corners are square, with no gradients.

**Layout**

A full-width solid blue header band across the top 12.5% of the slide holds a two-line left-aligned white title starting at x 3.8%. Below it, a centred bold chart title sits above a single chart plot area spanning roughly x 21.5% to 85%, with a left y-axis title, a right y-axis title and a centred legend row at about y 85%. The footer has the @KPCB logo at bottom left, the source line beside it and the page number '18' at bottom right, with no slide-number box or footer rule.

**Visuals**

Chart: combined stacked column and line chart titled 'Global Internet Advertising, 2009 – 2014'. Left axis titled 'Global Internet Advertising ($B)' runs from $0 to $150 in $25 steps. Right axis titled 'Y/Y Growth' runs from 0% to 25% in 5% steps. Category axis shows 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014. Stacked series 'Desktop Advertising' (bottom, blue) and 'Mobile Advertising' (top, red). Printed stack totals: 2009 $59, 2010 $70, 2011 $85, 2012 $100, 2013 $117, 2014 $133. Desktop values are not printed; about $56 (2009), about $67 (2010), about $80 (2011), about $91 (2012), about $103 (2013), about $114 (2014). Mobile values are not printed; about $3 (2009), about $3 (2010), about $5 (2011), about $9 (2012), about $14 (2013), about $19 (2014). Line series 'Y/Y Growth' (green, about 3 px stroke with small markers) on the right axis: no point for 2009; about 19% (2010), about 22.5% (2011), about 17% (2012), about 17.5% (2013), about 13.5% (2014). No points are highlighted. Gridlines are dashed grey horizontals at each $25 step. Legend below the plot: blue square 'Desktop Advertising', red square 'Mobile Advertising', green line 'Y/Y Growth'. Logo: @KPCB green wordmark bottom left.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF. White background #FFFFFF with a full-width blue title band #00689D. Title text white #FFFFFF in Arial regular (Helvetica-like sans-serif), size 4.44% of slide height, two lines. Chart title, axis titles, tick labels, data labels and legend text are black #000000 Arial Bold, 2.6% of slide height (chart title 3.33%). Accents: desktop bars #00689D, mobile bars #DC3C2E, growth line green #00B050. Source line Arial regular 1.29% in black; page number Arial regular 1.84% in #353B37. Bars are flat with no shadows, gradients or rounded corners. Gridlines dashed mid-grey #808080 0.75 pt; baseline axis line grey.

### Slide 32

**Review notes**

- Worth studying: A simple then-and-now layout, with a small image on each side and one-line takeaways, turns a category shift into an instantly understood story.
- Review: Most charts are readable and well matched to the claim, such as the stacked bars on slides 15 and 25 and the market cap tables on slide 7, and the then-and-now panels on slides 32 to 45 make the enterprise case at a glance.
- Worth keeping: Keep the takeaway-style title bars, the consistent source line, and the then-and-now panel layout with a one-line benefit caption (slide 32).

**Layout**

Full-width blue header band across the top 12.5% of the slide holds a two-line left-aligned title starting at about 3.8% from the left. Below it, two equal columns are split by a thin vertical grey divider at about x 50%: the left column is headed THEN (centred over the left photo) and the right column is headed NOW (centred over the right device image). A thin horizontal grey rule spans about 5% to 95% of the width at about 81.7% height, with a centred one-line takeaway beneath it. The @KPCB logo and source line sit at the bottom left, and the page number '35' sits at the bottom right, about 96% from the left.

**Visuals**

Two photographs and one device composite, no chart or table. Left photograph: a close-up of a hand holding a black and gold fountain pen, signing a printed financial sheet with a blue ink signature; the sheet shows columns of numbers including 74,727.8, 71,536.3, 3,156.8, 629.1, 1,083.1 and 75,804.7, a printed '79' at right, and the page is white/pale grey with warm skin tones on the hand. The shallow depth of field blurs the foreground fingers and background, and the photo is a plain rectangle (not full-bleed, not cropped to a shape, no overlay or tint). Right composite: a black iPad in landscape, with a dark bezel and a blue app bar showing Sales Contract (1), a status bar reading 3:30 PM, and a toolbar with Drag & Drop onto Document, Signature, Initial, My Name, Date Signed, Text and Company buttons. The iPad screen displays a Device Install Sheet document with a blue header reading Device Install Sheet and Med Device International logo (a blue-and-white node mark with the words Med Device International), and a bulleted Device Checklist (Read and understand, Equipment required for the transaction in good working condition, Startup/shutdown procedures, Cleaning, exterior and optics Patient alignment and head position, Seating and table requirements, Exam flow and purpose of steps). Over the document is a Draw Your Signature dialog with a blue Cancel and Adopt button, a white signing pad with blue handwritten Tom Wood signature on a dashed line, pen tools, and black, blue and red colour swatches, plus a small line of fine print. Behind and to the right of the iPad a black smartphone is partly hidden, showing a blue and yellow screen edge. The composite has a soft grey floor shadow under the tablet. The logo at bottom left is the green @KPCB wordmark.

**Design**

Background: Solid white (#FFFFFF) background with a blue (#00689D) header band across the top. White background with a solid blue header band (#00689D) across the top. Title and subtitle text in white (#FFFFFF) regular sans-serif (Arial/Helvetica style) on the band. THEN and NOW headings in black (#000000) bold Arial, about 4.4% of slide height. Column subheads and the takeaway line are black (#000000) regular Arial, about 3.3% and 2.8% of slide height. Source line is black Arial about 1.3%. Page number is dark grey (#353B37) Arial about 1.8%. Accent colours: header blue #00689D, divider and rule in mid grey (#8C8C8C approx.), logo green (#3DBA7E approx.). Shapes have no rounded corners; the divider and rule are plain 1 px grey lines. The photo has no border or shadow; the iPad has rounded black bezel corners with a soft drop shadow.

**Visuals**

Left (THEN): a network diagram, about 688 by 600 px, showing a hub-and-spoke style set of connected nodes. There are five message-window icons, each a rounded rectangle with three dots at top and three horizontal text lines. YOUR APP is a yellow-green (#D4D92E) icon at top centre with its label above it. HELPDESK is a purple (#7B68B8) icon at upper right with its label above. LIVE CHAT is a red-orange (#E05A3A) icon at left with its label to the left. MARKETING AUTOMATION is a grey-teal (#7C918E) icon at centre with its label above. CRM is a green (#3DB574) icon at lower left-centre with its label above. EMAIL MARKETING is an orange (#F2A93B) icon at lower right with its label to the right. Each icon is linked by double-headed black curved arrows to one or more person nodes: dark navy (#243247) filled circles with a white person silhouette, and light blue (#CDE8F7) filled circles with a navy silhouette. There are about 14 person nodes in total, with dark nodes near the outer icons and light nodes between them. Arrows connect nodes in a loop around the icons, with no legend and no highlighted points. Right (NOW): a product screenshot, about 588 by 375 px, of the Intercom desktop web app on a white background, with a dark-bordered window frame and a blue top navigation bar (#0B6DB0) showing People (2,498), Companies (345), Conversations (3,146), Manual and Auto tabs. The left sidebar is light grey (#F2F4F6) with USER DATA filters (NAME, EMAIL, USER ID, SIGNED UP, LAST SEEN) and radio buttons for RELATIVE (more than, exactly, less than 30 days ago) and ABSOLUTE (after, on, before), plus blue buttons Save Segment... and Auto Message.... The main table header reads 372 / 839 users with columns NAME and EMAIL, and rows include Tom Bacon at Book (tom@book...), Claire Holmes at TRP (claire@trp...), Kelvin Diaz at Hub (kelvin@hub...), Dave Concannon at Hosted and 1 other (dave@grap...), Leah Schuster at Donate (leah@50...), César Sepúlveda at Canal 13 Inte... and 2 others (cesar@mec...), Alex von Oech at Lay (a@lay.com), Anna Huston at Vestor (anna@vest...), Tom Barclay at Rosemary Co... (tom.barclay...), Casey at Scratch (casey@trys...), Austin Campbell at Sellbrite (acampbell...). Overlaid at lower right is a black smartphone mockup, about 1.2 times the height of the phone frame, showing a conversation with Janed Abbott at the top, a grey message from Matt Hodges asking to look at a trial, and a blue outgoing message reading Hi Janet, It looks like you have reached the limit for teammates on your current plan. You'll need to upgrade to add more collaborators. To do so, simply click Upgrade in your ProjectMap settings. Cheers, Matt. with a Write a reply... field below. **Visuals**

Two illustrations and one logo. Left: a circular composition (about 28.8% by 38% of the slide) of a cartoon businessman in a dark charcoal suit, white shirt and bright blue tie, standing with arms outstretched in a multi-armed pose, with brown hair and brown shoes. He is surrounded by a ring of small flat icons: a wall clock at top, a clipboard with green lines upper left, a dark grey coffee mug upper right, a calendar showing 25 at right, a smartphone with a green rising-line chart at lower left, a tablet/monitor with a bar chart and magnifier at lower right, a blue sneaker at the bottom, plus thin blue arcs, dotted network diagrams and small circles and dots. The circle sits on a very light grey grid-textured background, and the illustration is not boxed. Right: two smartphone mockups, the front one in white with a grey outline showing the Gainsight app: status bar reading AT&T, 9:35 AM, 97% battery; blue header with the word Gainsight and a bell icon; a back arrow, the customer name Abbett and a blue Save All button. Below are five rows: a red Overall tile showing 48 beside a grey speech bubble reading Abbett has made tremendous strides with our product, increasing their usage by 25% year over year. They've seen a 20% increase in their; a green Sponsor tile 76 with a slider marked 76 in a green circle; a red Support tile 48 with slider marked 48 in a red circle; a yellow Engagement tile 58 with slider marked 58 in a yellow circle; a red Usage tile 49 with slider marked 49 in a red circle. A second, partly hidden phone sits behind on the right showing a Record panel, an Engagement panel with 2 Weeks selector, a navy line chart with Sep '14 and Oct '14 axis labels, Karl Jones and integration Act... rows. Accents: KPCB green around #3DB87A; the divider and rule are mid grey #8C8C8C at about 1 pt. Illustration palette uses blues (#2E9BD6), navy (#1F3A5F), charcoal (#3A3A3A) and skin/brown tones. **Layout**

A full-width solid blue title band runs across the top 12.5% of the slide, with a two-line left-aligned white title starting at about 3.8% from the left edge. Below it, a borderless table is centred horizontally between about 18.7% and 88% of the slide width, with a row-label column on the left, two logo/value columns (Facebook Messenger and Snapchat) and thin grey horizontal rules between rows. A small KPCB wordmark sits bottom-left with the source line beside it, and the page number 51 sits bottom-right at about 96% x and 95% y.

**Visuals**

Table with three header-label rows (Name, Launch, Primary Country) in the left column and two columns. Column 1 Facebook Messenger: logo above, name Facebook Messenger, launch August 2011, primary country Global. Column 2 Snapchat: logo above, name Snapchat, launch September 2011, primary country Global. Rows (label: Facebook Messenger | Snapchat): Messaging: Separate messaging app (2014) | Chat (2014). Group Messaging: green check mark | red cross. Voice Calls: VoIP voice calls in US (2013) | red cross. Video Calls / Chat: Free VoIP video calls (2015) | Video Chat (2014). Payments: Messenger Payments (2015) | Snapcash (2014). Stickers: Sticker support (2013) | red cross. Games: red cross | red cross. Commerce: Businesses on Messenger (2015) | red cross. Media: red cross | Discover (2015). QR Codes: red cross | QR Codes to add friends (2015). Food Delivery: red cross | red cross. Taxi Services: red cross | red cross. User Stories / Moments: red cross | Shared Stories (2013). Developer Platform: Messenger Platform (2015) | red cross. Two logos: the Facebook Messenger app icon (a blue speech bubble with a white lightning-bolt stroke, gradient from cyan to blue, about 91 by 91 px, about 6% wide) and the Snapchat app icon (white ghost outline on a glossy yellow rounded square, about 90 by 88 px, about 6% wide). KPCB wordmark: '@KPCB' in green bold letters, about 7.5% wide.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF background. White background with a solid #00689D blue title band across the top. Title and subtitle are white regular Arial-style sans-serif at about 4.4% of slide height, title in two lines. Table labels and column headers are black bold Arial-style sans-serif at about 1.7% of slide height. Table values are bold green #00B050 Arial-style sans-serif at about 1.7%. Check and cross marks use Wingdings glyphs at about 2.8%, green #00B050 for the check and red #FF0000 for crosses. Thin mid-grey horizontal rules (about #A6A6A6, about 0.1% of slide height) separate rows. Source line is about 1.3% of slide height black Arial. Page number is dark grey #353B37 Arial at about 1.8%. No corner radii, shadows or gradients on the table; the logos carry their own gradients.

### Slide 53

**Text**

In Messaging, Not One-Size-Fits-All, For Now...
Many People Use Different Messaging Apps for Various Purposes
One User...
(Illustrative)
...Another User
(Illustrative)
Kik
KakaoTalk
Snapchat
52
Image: Stratechery (right), BoumanBlog (left).

**Layout**

A full-width blue title band runs across the top of the slide with a two-line white title left-aligned near the top-left margin. Below it two equal columns sit side by side, each with a bold centred heading and an italic '(Illustrative)' sub-heading above a square-cornered app-folder image; a small green @KPCB logo sits bottom-left with a source line beside it and the page number bottom-right.

**Visuals**

Two illustrative photographs of smartphone home-screen app folders, presented as screenshots of app icons in a 3x3 grid. Left folder (One User...): on a teal-to-aqua gradient background inside a rounded folder panel, icons in order: Kik (dark charcoal speech bubble with green 'kik.' lettering, label 'Kik'), Messages (green speech bubble, label 'Messages'), LINE (green icon with white 'LINE' bubble and red badge '2', label 'LINE'), WhatsApp (green phone bubble, label 'WhatsApp'), Hangouts (white icon with green quote marks and red badge '1', label 'Hangouts'), KakaoTalk (yellow square with dark 'TALK' bubble, label 'KakaoTalk'), WeChat (green icon with two white speech bubbles, label 'WeChat'), Messenger (white square with blue lightning bolt bubble, label 'Messenger'), Snapchat (yellow square with white ghost, label 'Snapchat'). Right folder (...Another User): on a pastel gradient background of peach, pink, lavender and mint inside a rounded folder panel, icons in order: Snapchat (yellow with white ghost, label 'Snapchat'), Viber (purple phone handset, label 'Viber'), WhatsApp (green phone bubble, label 'WhatsApp'), Tango (red-orange square with white T, label 'Tango'), LINE (green bubble with white 'LINE' text, label 'LINE'), Path (red square with white P, label 'Path'), whisper (purple circular icon with silhouette, label 'whisper'), Voxer (orange square with white walkie-talkie, label 'Voxer'), Hangouts (white square with green quote marks, label 'Hangouts'). A row of four small page-indicator dots sits near the bottom of the right folder, first dot white and filled. Both images are fully visible, rectangular, unboxed and uncropped, with soft shadows on the icons; the photographs are evenly lit with no overlay.

**Design**

Background: White #FFFFFF.

Top navigation bar reads 'Watch'. Behind the dialog are dimmed live-stream thumbnails with red 'LIVE' tags and a viewer count '2'. The dialog is a white rounded box with a light blue square close button marked with a white X at its top-right corner. Its header band shows three overlapping circles: a blurred-edge circle of the Palace of Fine Arts rotunda with its reflecting pond, a dark circle with a white audio waveform, and a circle with a street map showing a red location dot. Below them the title 'Start a Broadcast' in bold dark grey, then 'We need a few things before you can broadcast.' in light grey. Three outlined teal pill buttons with thin teal borders: 'Enable Camera' with a camera icon, 'Enable Microphone' with a microphone icon, 'Enable Location' with a location arrow icon. Beneath them in small light grey text: 'Don't worry, you can choose to hide your location before each broadcast.' The bottom of the screen shows a dark tab bar with a teal TV icon, a dark record-style icon with a red dot, and a grey people icon. Dominant colours: white dialog, teal #2A8FA8 accents, dark brown-grey dimmed background, warm brown photo tones.

Three-column grid under a full-width blue header band. The title sits left-aligned inside the band, with its left edge near 3.8% of slide width. **Visuals**

Eleven photographs and logos in three columns. Left column: (1) a photo of a crowded airport-style check-in hall with travellers queuing along a counter, shot from a low wide angle under warm ceiling lights, with a tiled beige floor; (2) the Airbnb wordmark with its coral Bélo symbol; (3) a close-up photo of a hand holding a gold-edged smartphone showing an Airbnb listing 'Cozy Bedroom in Spacious Du...' in Chicago with a blue-walled bedroom photo and a '$50' price badge, the phone held against a brown blurred background. Middle column: (4) an overhead photo of a long queue of people on a city sidewalk beside a row of yellow taxicabs in traffic, with a concrete barrier; (5) a street photo of a woman with shopping bags raising a hand beside an open yellow taxi on a wet city street, with a man in a dark jacket beside her; (6) the Uber wordmark with a black square U-logo at left; (7) a screenshot of a white smartphone showing the Uber 'CONFIRMATION' screen at 11:38 AM with 'Uber HQ 405 Howard St, San Francisco', a beige street map with a green pin, and a 'VISA PERSONAL •••• 5555' payment row and 'FARE ESTIMATE' and 'PROMO CODE' buttons at the bottom, cropped at the bottom edge. Right column: (8) a photo of a large car park full of parked cars seen from above, mostly silver, black and red; (9) a photo of a woman in a grey blazer holding jars at a grocery shelf of produce with 'ORGANIC' price tags; (10) the Instacart wordmark in green script; (11) a photo of a hand holding a white smartphone showing the Instacart+ grid of produce, over a dark green cutting mat with red tomatoes and lettuce. Footer: the @KPCB logo in green letters, which is a small raster image. Photos are rectangular, unrounded and boxed, with no overlays, tints or borders. Overall lighting is natural and mixed, with dominant colours of yellow, grey, red and green.

Accent colours come from the logos: Airbnb coral #FF5A5F, Uber black #000000, Instacart green #43B17A, KPCB logo green #3DB58A. Divider rules are mid grey #A0A0A0, about 2 px wide. Subject: a single-rotor agricultural unmanned helicopter with a white cylindrical tank, red and orange hoses, a yellow nozzle fitting, grey skid landing gear, and two long horizontal spray booms with orange-tipped nozzles, hovering low over a field. The field shows rows of ploughed brown soil alternating with bright green crop seedlings receding toward the horizon. Spray mist drifts from the nozzles beneath the booms. The background is hazy and out of focus, with bare trees, low pale buildings with tiled roofs, and a grey sky. Composition: the drone sits in the upper-middle of the frame, slightly right of centre, with the furrows leading the eye from the bottom edge toward it. Lighting is soft, diffuse and overcast with no hard shadows. Dominant colours: green, earthy brown, grey-white, with white and orange on the drone. No overlay or tint. The photograph is a box with square corners and no border. Logo: the @KPCB wordmark at bottom left, in green.

### Slide 89

**Text**

Cyber Attacks = Growing Bigger / Faster...
•
Insider Misuse = Significant Cause of Breaches
>20% of breaches come directly from insiders with malicious intent. In most
breaches, attackers have foothold within internal networks & spread / steal data
through privilege abuse / credential misuse.
•
Mobile Devices = Increasingly Used to Harvest Data
Adware grew 136% to 410,000 apps between 2013 and first three quarters of
2014, giving attackers access to personal information such as contacts, which
can subsequently be used to launch phishing attacks.
•
Mobile Device Management = Critical in Preventing Breaches
22% of breaches reported by network security decision makers involve lost /
stolen devices.

Source: “Millennials at Work: Reshaping the Workplace,” by PWC, 2011, Global.
Survey of 4,364 graduates across 75 countries. All respondents were aged 31 or under and had graduated between 2008 and 2011.
Millennials defined as those born between 1980 and 2000. In 2015, they are ages 15-35.

**Layout**

Full-width blue header band across the top 12.5% of the slide holds a two-line white title left-aligned at about x 3.8%, with the first line at y 1.9% and the second at y 6.7%. Below it, a centred two-line chart heading sits above a horizontal bar chart whose category labels are right-aligned in a column ending near x 32%, with bars starting at a common baseline x 33.3% and running down from y 28% to y 88%. Footer: @KPCB logo bottom-left at x 1.8%, three-line source note starting at x 9.8%, page number 110 bottom-right at x 95.4%, y 95.4%. Margins about 2% left and right, with the chart area ending near x 96%.

**Visuals**

Chart: horizontal bar chart, single series, 15 bars, all in teal #00A9AF with no highlighted bar. Chart title: 'Which Three Benefits Would You Most Value From an Employer?' (bold italic black) with subtitle '% Ranking Each 1st Place, Global' (bold italic black, smaller). Value axis: percent, scale 0% to 25% implied by vertical dashed gridlines every 5% (at 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%), no printed axis title or tick labels. Category axis: vertical grey line at the bar baseline with short tick marks between categories. Values printed at each bar end, all printed, none estimated: Training and Development 22%; Flexible Working Hours 19%; Cash Bonuses 14%; Free Private Healthcare 8%; Pension Scheme or Other Retirement Funding 6%; Greater Vacation Allowance 6%; Financial Assistance with Housing 5%; Company Car 4%; Assistance in Clearing Debts Incurred While Studying 3%; Maternity / Paternity Benefits 3%; Subsidized Travel Costs 2%; Free Child Care 2%; Access to Low Interest Loans / Borrowing Options 2%; Time Off to Do Community / Charity Work 1%; I'd Prefer No Benefits and Higher Wages 4%. Bar lengths scale at about 50 px per percentage point on the 2000 px wide image. No legend. Logo: '@KPCB' wordmark in green about #3DB884, at bottom-left, the '@' in lighter weight and 'KPCB' in bold sans-serif capitals, not boxed.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF. Plain white background. Header band solid #00689D with white regular sans-serif title (Arial/Helvetica regular) about 4.3% of slide height for each line, no caps. Chart heading in Arial Bold Italic black #000000: main line about 3.3% of slide height, subtitle about 2.6%. Category and value labels in Arial Bold #353B37 (dark grey), category labels 1.84% and value labels 2.60%. Gridlines dashed mid-grey about #8C8C8C, thin. Baseline and category axis line solid grey about #8C8C8C, thin. No corner radii.

### Slide 112

**Text**

Millennials Expect Flexibility & Like Technology @ Work
Millennials =
Expect Flexible Work Hours
Millennials =
Tech Savvy
•Many = expect to be mobile & work from home / office / cafes at will.
•~20% = identify as ‘night owls’ (often work outside normal business hours).
•38% = freelancing vs. 32% among those over 35 years old.
•32% = believe they will be working ‘mainly flexible hours’ in future.
•34% = prefer to collaborate online at work as opposed to in-person or via phone (vs. 19% for older generations).
•45% = use personal smartphones for work purposes (vs. 18% for older generations).
•41% = likely to download applications to use for work purposes in next 12 months & use their own money to pay for them (vs. 24% for older generations).
@KPCB
Source: “Freelancing in America,” Survey of 5,000 Working Americans commissioned by Freelancer’s Union and Upwork (formerly Elance-oDesk), 9/14, USA.

### Slide 133

**Text**

Many People =
Use Online Platforms / Marketplaces to Supplement Income
Select Online Platforms – Personal Impact
• 72% = NYC hosts depend on Airbnb earnings to pay rent / mortgage...50%+ = NYC hosts / are freelancers or other non-traditional workers supplementing income... / • 80-90% = Global Airbnb hosts occasionally rent out their own home to supplement income
• 82% = Sellers are part-time (ie: have jobs outside of Etsy) / • 26% = Sellers have full-time jobs (outside of Etsy)...48% = independent / part-time / / temporary workers / • 36% = Use Etsy earnings to cover household expenses...24% for discretionary spend
• 37% = Pros are part-time with income supplemented by other sources
• 74% = Drive to maintain steady income as other income sources unstable / unpredictable / • 61% = Have another job...31% = full-time on another job; 30% = part-time job apart from / Uber; 38% = no other job
• 68% = People who said earning extra money is a motivation for freelancing / • 80% = Non-freelancers willing to do work outside primary job to make more money / • 60%+ = Freelancers provide at least 1/2 household income
132
Source: “An Analysis of the Labor Market for Uber’s Driver-Partners in the United States,” Uber, 1/15. Note Uber data are USA only.
“The Tremendous Impact of Airbnb in New York,” Airbnb, 5/15. Additional data are from Airbnb.
“Redefining Entrepreneurship: Etsy Sellers’ Economic Impact”, 11/13. Published by Etsy. Survey measured 5,500 USA-based sellers on Etsy’s marketplace. Note Etsy data is USA only.
Upwork (formerly Elance-oDesk) Annual Impact Report, 2014.
“Freelancing in America,” Survey of 5,000 Working Americans commissioned by Freelancer’s Union and Upwork (formerly Elance-oDesk), 9/14. USA.
Thumbtack, 2015.
Note percentages may not add up to 100% owing to rounding.

MBO Partners defines workers in the in the “On-Demand Economy,” as those who generate economic activity through the use of online platforms and marketplaces that help customers quickly
connect and transact with suppliers of goods and services. These include services like Airbnb, Uber, Lyft, Handy, Etsy, TaskRabbit, and many others.
* NOTE: MBO study only includes on-demand workers who devote at least one hour per week to an on-demand platform. Those who use these platforms less frequently are not counted. Figure has
been de-duplicated.

Online Platforms / Marketplaces =
Benefits & Challenges for Consumers
Benefits
Challenges
Choice / Access – product depth +
breadth...availability of goods / services /

Time Savings – can offset incremental
costs, if any
Transparency – ability to research / set
expectations / track process
Personalized – can get items / services
on own schedule
Online Reputation & Trust Systems
Often in Place – ability to read & write
reviews / ratings for merchants & service
providers
Time / Cost Tradeoff – Products with
rapid delivery may be more expensive
Quality – unable to test products /
services...reliant on feedback from
peers / reviews
Trust – new marketplaces must prove
trustworthiness to consumers
Time / Convenience Tradeoff –
Convenience of delivery to home /
work may mean delaying gratification
of getting product immediately
@KPCB
Source: Various.

### Slide 139

**Text**

Online Platforms / Marketplaces =
Benefits & Challenges for Workers
Benefits
Challenges
Financial – ability to earn supplemental / primary income
Flexibility – choose own schedule / task, location / income goals-targets
Skill Set Match – can often effectively match skills with needed services
Feedback / Communication – often real-time / direct
Data – customer location + data can allow workers to provide more informed / efficient service
Customer Base – marketplaces can aggregate demand that may be fragmented / far-reaching (global)
Growth – rising sector demand for services should boost opportunities / competition for workers
Incumbent Displacement – creates change / uncertainty
Financial – lack of predictable income possible
Uncertainty – lack of clarity related to demand / work / reporting possible
Benefits Clarity – insurance / vacation / sick leave / pension...
Asset Use – potential job requirement to use personal items (cars / phones...)
Training / Development – potentially limited training / development / supervision
Workplace Culture – people often dispersed
138

remove bad actors

their jobs – effectively regulate what they had intended to regulate all along.
@KPCB

X-axis: years 1990 to 2015 YTD, labels rotated about 45 degrees, with 2012* and 2014** footnote markers. Series 1: Technology IPO Volume ($B), green stacked segment on top of each bar. ### Slide 176

**Text**

Technology-Related Company Investing Observations
•
Booms / Busts – In periods of material business disruption – like
those brought about by the evolutions of the Internet – company
creation typically goes through a boom → bust → boom-let cycle
while wealth creation typically goes through a boom-let → bust →
boom cycle.
•
Valuations – There are pockets of Internet company overvaluation
but there are also pockets of undervaluation – the one rule is that
very few companies will win – those that do – can win big.
•
Platforms – Race is won by those that build platforms & drive free
cash flow over long-term (a decade or more).
•
Free Cash Flow – Value of a business, over time, is the present
value of its future cash flows.

**Layout**

Three equal columns centred at roughly 17%, 50% and 83% of the slide width, each holding a bold heading, an italic two-line subtitle, a screenshot or phone image, and a body paragraph set below. A full-width blue title bar fills the top 12.5% of the slide, with the two-line title left-aligned at about 3.8% from the left edge. The KPCB logo sits bottom-left at about 1.8% from the left edge and the page number 182 sits bottom-right at about 95% across and 95% down. Margins are roughly 2 to 4% on each side; there is no separate footer band.

**Visuals**

Three screenshot or photo panels and several magenta annotation shapes. (1) Google column: a cropped screenshot of the Google homepage with the Google logo in its standard multicolour wordmark, a search box containing the word complexity, two grey buttons labelled Google Search and I'm Feeling Lucky, a magenta-to-transparent gradient wedge (#FF00FF fading to white) drooping from the search box to the right, and beneath it a search results list with blue links and green URLs, followed by a row of four small grey-scale thumbnails labelled Images for complexity. (2) Instagram column: a tall phone screenshot of the Instagram feed in blue header (#00689D-like) showing a building facade photo with a lamp post and a window grille, a heart icon and 112 likes, plus an overlapping dark camera-screen screenshot showing a black laptop-style keyboard with a magenta rectangle outline framing the keys T, Y, U, I, O, G, H, J, K, L, B, N, M, and a blue shutter button with a camera icon; a magenta line runs from the keyboard frame down-left to the Instagram body text. (3) Tinder column: a tall phone screenshot of the Tinder app with grey interface, a tinder wordmark in red-orange, and a photo of a smiling woman with long light-brown hair in a dark jacket and scarf gesturing upward in front of a grey sky and building; a yellow-outlined OOPS stamp is over the photo; the bottom row shows red X, green heart and blue pin icons in circles. A thick magenta outlined rotated square frames the card and a magenta curved arrow points left toward the woman. A faint pale grey panel sits under the Tinder column and a faint pale image sits under the Google column. Colours are dominant white, black text, blue #00689D header, magenta #FF00FF accents, and the grey and blue of the screenshots. Photos are not cropped beyond their screenshot edges, appear boxed with no border, and the magenta items overlay them at about 78% opacity.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF, with a blue #00689D bar across the top 12.5%. White slide background (#FFFFFF) with a full-width blue header bar #00689D across the top 12.5%. Title text is white (#FFFFFF) regular Arial-style sans-serif, about 4.4% of slide height. Column headings are black (#000000) Arial Bold at about 3.3% of slide height. Subtitles are black (#000000) Arial Italic at about 2.6%. Body text is black (#000000) Arial regular at about 1.5% of slide height, with MS PGothic for curly quotes. Page number is #353B37 Arial at about 1.8%. KPCB logo is green (#3DB37A approximately). Accent colour is magenta #FF00FF used on annotation shapes and gradient wedge. Shapes have square corners, no visible shadows, and no gradient except the magenta wedge that fades out. Lines are thin magenta strokes of roughly 1 to 2 px width.

YOUR TRIP
OCTOBER 21, 2015 AT 4:29 PM
$8
TRIP SUMMARY
RATE YOUR RIDE
Most imaging applications asked to turn on the camera, whereas Snapchat began the interaction in live camera mode. The invitation to snap a photo was immediate; and the secretive, self-destruct feature completed the addictive loop.

Analogy: A hammer’s handle invites you to grasp it. In the design world that’s called an object’s “affordance” — it primes how you might use it.

Removing cash or a card payment from a taxi transaction was a huge technical innovation that achieved a better designed outcome. It’s often easy to hope that design can solve a fundamental problem — technology is what enables quantum leaps.

Analogy: When cars were rear-wheel drive, the “hump” in the back seat was a bummer. Front-wheel drive cars completely removed that constraint.

By keeping the entire interaction in view, and easily referred to within a vertical scroll, the experience of inputting information feels less like the computer is in control; and leads to completion rates of survey information with an average of 60% (vs 10%).

Analogy: The acclaimed film “Birdman” used the cinematic illusion of “the single take” to achieve a similar effect to create greater viewer immersion.
@KPCB

**Layout**

Three equal columns of centred headings, photos and body paragraphs sit below a full-width blue header band holding a two-line left-aligned title. Each column has a bold name, an italic subtitle, a visual at about 33.5% to 72.5% of slide height, and a left-aligned body paragraph at the bottom. The @KPCB logo sits bottom-left and the page number 183 bottom-right, both on a white margin of about 2% to 4% of slide width.

**Visuals**

Three photographs or screenshots, one per column. Column 1 (Snapchat): a photograph of a hand holding a white smartphone in live camera mode, pointing at a grey-blue stone on a grey-green slate surface, with a white speckled rock and an orange-brown rock beside it; a black wristwatch on the wrist; a pink Snapchat ghost logo in the upper-left corner over the white rock; natural daylight from above; slightly warm and muted greens and greys; the photo is a boxed rectangle, not full-bleed. Column 2 (Uber): a flat render of a black-bezel smartphone with a white screen showing the Uber 'YOUR TRIP' receipt: '$8' large in a light sans-serif, a small car icon and a map-pin map icon in grey circles under 'TRIP SUMMARY', a zig-zag torn-edge receipt divider and a grey 'RATE YOUR RIDE' area with five small pink-outlined yellow-orange stars overlaid across the bottom edge of the phone; white background around the phone, boxed. Column 3 (Typeform): a browser window screenshot with red-dot window controls and the URL http://typeform.com, showing a web form on a grey panel with red text, a red 'Ok' button, a red 'No problem' button and a red 'Create your own Typeform...' button; a faint washed-out ghost of the page behind it; a vertical pink double-headed arrow to the right of the screenshot running from about y 35% to y 72.5%. Faint ghost copies of other images sit behind the slide in pale grey and are barely visible. The @KPCB logo is a green wordmark ('@KPCB', rounded sans-serif, green about #3BAA6B) at bottom left.

**Design**

Background: Solid white #FFFFFF background with a blue header band #00689D across the top 12.5%. Clean white background with a solid blue header band (#00689D) across the top 12.5% of the slide. Title text is white (#FFFFFF) in regular-weight Arial-like sans-serif, about 4.4% of slide height for the lines of the title. Column names are bold Arial-like sans-serif in black (#000000), about 3.3% of slide height. Subtitles are italic Arial-like sans-serif in black (#000000), about 2.6% of slide height. Body text is regular Arial-like sans-serif in black (#000000), about 1.5% of slide height, with about 1.5% line spacing. Page number is Arial-like regular in dark grey-green #353B37, about 1.8% of slide height. Accent colours: pink #E8177F for the Snapchat ghost logo and the vertical arrow, and orange-yellow #F5A623 for the stars. Shapes have no rounded corners, no shadows and no gradients.

### Slide 186

**Text**

US Healthcare in the 21st Century
Purchase + Delivery Change Forever
ACA and Government Effects
• With Cadillac tax coming into effect in 2018, employers are moving towards offering high deductible health benefit plans
• 72% of employers offer at least 1 consumer directed health plan
• 30% of Medicare payments will be tied to quality or value by end of 2016 and 50% by end of 2018
• Effective Jan 2015, Medicare has separate payments for chronic care management for “non-face-to-face” care
Major Healthcare Purchasers
Private Health
($947 Bn)
Out of Pocket
($338 Bn)
Medicare - Medicaid
($1,040 Bn)
Traditional Healthcare Consumer
Doctor’s Office
Hospital
Urgent Care
21st Century Consumption
Connected Medicine
Retail
Healthcare Apps and Wearables
Healthcare Exchanges
Source: Beth Seidenberg, KPCB General Partner and Lynne Chou, KPCB Partner. Sources: CMS National Health Expenditure Projections 2013-2023, National Business Group Survey Aug. 2014

### Slide 190

**Text**

Consumer / Commercial Drone Development –
Ranking Countries by Government Accommodation...
1) France & United Kingdom
• Both countries allow Beyond Visual Line of Sight “BVLOS” commercial operations.
• In France, users must obtain a proper pilot’s license plus 100 hours of flying experience &
20 hours of drone training.
• In United Kingdom, operator must be approved by the Civil Aviation Authority “CAA.”
• France & UK both have training certifications, weight categories & relatively mature regulatory
framework.
2) Canada
• Early to allow commercial operations with Special Flight Operating Certificates and regulator
takes holistic safety approach without requiring pilots licenses. In November 2014, Transport
Canada issued blanket exemptions for drones weighing less than 2kgs, but restrictions are tight
whereby UAVs 2kg or less have to avoid flying closer than 9km from build-up areas (e.g. group
of buildings larger than a farmstead).
• Still lacks a comprehensive regulatory framework.
3) Australia
• Australia has a mature regulatory framework, but Civil Aviation and Safety Authority “CASA” is
rewriting its regulations with the concept of a micro UAS rule. Yamaha has had success in
Australia with its R-MAX unmanned helicopter.
4) Japan
• Led way on UAVs 20 years ago with development of the Yamaha R-MAX, but country did not
develop regulatory structure, and has lost its early technical lead.
Source: News articles, KPCB analysis – Wen Hsieh / James Tang / Paul Yeh.

### Slide 191

**Text**

...Consumer / Commercial Drone Development –
Ranking Countries by Government Accommodation
5) USA
• FAA is about 6 months into an exemption program that grants company-by-company exemptions / (permits) for specific UAS applications. However, those permits come with restrictions & conditions that / pose impediments to operators, such as pilot certification (in a real aircraft), mandatory separation from / persons and structures (500 feet), a prohibition against night operations, & other parameters that are / generally viewed as overly conservative & potentially not capable of being satisfied by many of the / companies being granted those permits. Agency claims that statutes prohibit it from providing a more / reasonable approach to UAS permits.
• FAA is trying to speed up its processes, and is now up to ~400 exemptions granted to companies. / However, it still has a massive backlog with ~1,200 more pending. Additionally, the FAA is at least 18 / months away from actual small UAS rules.
6) China
• Military allots only 1/5 of airspace to civilian use and is very sensitive about drone usage. While there is / no blanket ban on commercial drone activity, China’s Civil Aviation Administration requires anyone / operating a drone >7kg to have a license. For flying drones <7kg, no license is required as long as it’s / below 400 feet and within operator’s line of sight. However, this policy has caused confusion among / operators and regulators. In one example, the Beijing Police briefly detained a well-known aerial / photographer for filming the Forbidden City - they confiscated his quadcopter and later returned it to the / photographer at the airport on his flight out of China.
•
Other countries developing UAS regulations
• Mexico recently released framework including micro UAS rule.
• New Zealand is behind but has proposed a solid risk-based set of regulations.
@KPCB
Source: News articles, KPCB analysis – Wen Hsieh / James Tang / Paul Yeh.

- text at x 13.9, y 59.5, w 75.1, h 2.2 [ArialMT; font size 2.22; #000000]: operating a drone >7kg to have a license. For flying drones <7kg, no license is required as long as it’s
- text at x 13.9, y 62.1, w 73.7, h 2.2 [ArialMT; font size 2.22; #000000]: below 400 feet and within operator’s line of sight. However, this policy has caused confusion among
- text at x 13.9, y 64.6, w 70.8, h 2.2 [ArialMT; font size 2.22; #000000]: operators and regulators. In one example, the Beijing Police briefly detained a well-known aerial
- text at x 6.6, y 76.4, w 0.7, h 2.6 [ArialMT; font size 2.60; #00689D]: •
- text at x 8.4, y 76.4, w 40.9, h 2.6 [Arial-BoldMT; font size 2.60; #00689D]: Other countries developing UAS regulations
- text at x 13.9, y 67.2, w 76.4, h 2.2 [ArialMT; font size 2.22; #000000]: photographer for filming the Forbidden City - they confiscated his quadcopter and later returned it to the
- text at x 13.9, y 69.7, w 38.9, h 2.2 [ArialMT; font size 2.22; #000000]: photographer at the airport on his flight out of China.
- text at x 12.1, y 79.7, w 47.6, h 2.2 [ArialMT; font size 2.22; #000000]: • Mexico recently released framework including micro UAS rule.
- text at x 12.1, y 82.6, w 59.1, h 2.2 [ArialMT; font size 2.22; #000000]: • New Zealand is behind but has proposed a solid risk-based set of regulations.
